title: Every money trap the middle class falls into, explained
cta: Which trap are you in? Comment the number

thumbnail.pattern: a person running on a treadmill or caught in machinery, the traps as things circled in red, one huge word with a question mark in a red box, and a big worried face at the side

references.what: a man running on a treadmill inside giant gears, TRAPPED? huge in a red box, a big worried face on the right
the traps as drawn things in red-ringed circles (car, house, shopping cart) under DON'T FALL FOR THESE
three huge stacked words, the last in a red box, a face on the right looking at the viewer

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan just got a raise. His treadmill got faster, but his bank balance didn't move. Why? Six money traps take the raise before he sees it. Here's how.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here they are: the life that grows, the new car, the safe cash, the small charges, the bigger house, and the worst one, saved for last.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Six traps? How many of them am I in right now?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Count them as we go. Most families I knew were caught in more than one, and none of them noticed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Each trap feels like a reward or a smart choice, which is exactly why it works, and why the treadmill keeps speeding up.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap one. The life that grows.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap one starts the day the raise lands: a nicer place, more takeout, and every bit of it feels earned.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Say his whole life costs {creep_amount} a month today: the rent, the food, the phone and the fun.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That sounds normal. So how is spending my own raise a trap?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Because prices climb: at an assumed {creep_inflation} a year, that same life costs {creep_new_monthly} a month in {creep_years} years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: His pay goes up with each raise, but his spending climbs by the same amount, so the gap between the two never grows.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Every year the rent, the groceries and the phone plan creep up, until the same life costs {creep_extra_month} more each month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And each new raise buys a bigger version of the same life, so the treadmill speeds up just to keep him in place.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: By then that's {creep_extra_year} more every year, just to live exactly the way he lives today.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's called lifestyle creep: each raise first covers rising prices, and spending the rest on a bigger life keeps the savings flat.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Over those {creep_years} years, the rising price of that same life adds up to {creep_extra_total} more than today's price.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: I watched it happen for my whole career. The raise was spent before the first new payslip ever arrived.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Then a different trap pulls into the driveway, shiny and new. So why does it still cost him money years after it stops being new?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap two. The new car.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: My old car still runs fine. But I earned a new one, right?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So he signs for a {car_amount} car, on a loan at an assumed {car_rate} a year, for {carval_years} years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's {car_emi} every month, and {car_interest} of it goes to interest, money that buys no car at all.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan pays {car_total_paid} in total over the loan, for a car with a sticker price of {car_amount}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Meanwhile the car loses value every year. At an assumed steady drop, after {carval_years} years it's worth {carval_final}.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. So I paid all that interest, and I'm left holding a car worth a fraction of the price?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the trap is the loop: the loan ends, the car looks old, he signs for a new one, and the payments start again.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: The car itself isn't the trap. Replacing it every few years, on a fresh loan each time, is what keeps him running.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A car is a depreciating asset: it loses value every year, and a loan adds interest on top of the loss.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Two traps, and both of them felt like rewards. So which trap would ever feel like being careful?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap three. The safe cash.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan is careful with his savings. He keeps {cash_amount} in a big-bank savings account paying an assumed {cash_rate} a year.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Cash in a bank can't lose. What could possibly go wrong with that?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: His bank pays him {cash_rate} a year, while prices climb at {cash_inflation}, so his cash falls a little further behind each year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Many big-bank savings accounts pay this little, because the bank lends that same money out to borrowers at much higher rates.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At {cash_rate} a year, in {cash_years} years his cash grows to only {cash_final}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Measured in today's money, that pile only buys what {cash_real_final} buys now.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So my safe money is actually shrinking while it sits there? How did I never notice?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Because the jar looks fuller every year, while the things it can buy melt away underneath it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's {cashloss_diff} of buying power gone in {cash_years} years, from money that never left the bank.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Cash is safe from a crash, yes. It just isn't safe from prices, and prices never take a year off.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At least Rohan can see that loss if he does the sum. So what about the charges so small he never even looks?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap four. The small charges that never stop.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Streaming, music, cloud storage, and a gym he rarely visits: each one takes a little every month.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: They're tiny, though. What's the harm in a few little apps?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Together they come to {subs_amount} a month, which is {subs_per_year_total} every single year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And because every charge renews by itself, he never decides to keep paying. The payments simply carry on.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The gym takes its fee every month, whether he goes or not, and he hasn't been since the spring.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Then there's the app he tried free for a week and forgot. The trial ended long ago, but the charge never did.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Over {subs_years} years, those little charges add up to {subs_total}, for things he barely uses.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rohan tries one question on each app: would he sign up again today? For half of them, the answer is no.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Subscriptions at least show up on a statement. But what about a charge that never shows up anywhere at all?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan finally invests. His {fund_amount} sits in a fund that charges an assumed {fund_fee_pct} a year.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Such a tiny percentage? Why would I ever worry about that?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On {fund_amount}, that's {fund_per_period} a year, and the fee is taken whether the fund does well or badly.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Even if the pot never grew, {fund_years} years of it is {fund_total} in fees, before counting the growth that money never got to earn.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The fee drips out of the fund every year, and every coin that leaves it stops growing for good.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the fee grows as the fund grows, because it's a share of the whole pot, not a flat charge.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Fund fees differ a lot, so the very same pot keeps far more of its own growth just by paying less for it.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The fee nobody reads is still a fee everybody pays, every year, in good markets and bad ones.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The name for it is the expense ratio, printed in the small print that so few people ever open.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's four traps you can spot once someone points at them. So what makes the last two so much harder to see?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap five. The bigger house.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But a house is an investment, isn't it? So a bigger house must be better.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A {small_amount} mortgage over {small_months} monthly payments, at an assumed {small_rate}, costs {small_emi} a month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Stretch to a {big_amount} house, and the payment jumps to {big_emi}, which is {housegap_diff} more every month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Across the whole loan, the bigger house costs {houseint_diff} more in interest alone, before the bigger bills for heat and repairs.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So what does the bigger house cost me in total, once every payment is made?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He pays {big_total_paid} for the bigger house in the end, against {small_total_paid} for the home he actually needs.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The extra room is never the expensive part. The extra payment is, every month of the loan, and every one comes with a bill.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: A house he can afford leaves room for every other goal. A house that stretches him leaves room for none.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: From the street, Rohan's bigger house looks like success.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Five traps so far, and each one costs money he can see. The last one costs nothing at all today. So why is it the worst?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Trap six. I'll start later.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I'll start investing when I earn more. What's the rush, really?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And this is the twist. Starting late, Rohan saves only {investdiff_diff} less in total. But at the end, he's {wait_diff} behind.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here's how. Plan A starts today. Plan B starts later. And both of them stop on exactly the same day, the day Rohan retires.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Plan A puts {early_amount} a month into investments for {early_years} years, growing at an assumed {early_rate} a year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: When he retires, all those small monthly amounts have grown into {early_final}, far more than he ever put in.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Plan B waits, then puts in the same amount for only {late_years} years. That grows to {late_final}, less than half as much.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Plan B puts in {late_invested} of his own money, and Plan A puts in {early_invested}: more, but not that much more on paper.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. I save almost the same money and still end up that far behind? How?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's because early money has years to earn on its own earnings, and those last years are where the tree grows biggest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: This is compounding, and the one thing it needs most is the one thing waiting takes away: time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: No bill ever arrives for waiting, yet it's the biggest cost on the list: {wait_diff}, just for starting later.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Every young man I lent money to thought time was the one thing he had plenty of. None of them was right.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Six traps: the creep, the car, the cash, the small charges, the house and later. Each one took a slice of every raise.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So that's why the raise never moved his balance: six traps took their share first. One rule for each, and Rohan finally steps off the treadmill.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's way out: he spends less than each raise, reads the fees, and starts early. So which trap are you in right now? Tell me the number.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Illustrative numbers with assumed rates. Which trap are you in? Comment the number below.

params.assumption: Illustrative amounts; inflation, loan, savings, fee and growth rates are assumed and held steady; before taxes; car value changes by an assumed {carval_rate} a year.
